findings.finding: The only application-wide middleware is SlowAPIMiddleware (rate limiting) and CORSMiddleware. No authentication middleware is applied globally. Auth is entirely opt-in per route via the require_approver dependency, and nothing enforces any route actually declares it.
findings.evidence: main.py:353-366 full middleware block, no third middleware exists. grep -rn "require_approver" backend/app returns exactly 4 files: rbac.py, auth/dependencies.py (definitions), epics.py, memory.py (the only 2 real usage sites).
findings.production_impact: jwt_auth_enabled=True protects nothing on its own -- it only changes require_approver's internal behavior for routes that already call it. Every mutating endpoint not explicitly depending on require_approver/get_current_user is reachable by any client regardless of auth config.
findings.recommendation: Add real global authentication enforcement (middleware with an explicit public-route allowlist, or a systematic per-route audit adding an auth dependency everywhere).
findings.fix_note: Added Depends(require_approver) or Depends(require_authenticated) to every mutating endpoint across all 13 API router files (~50 endpoints), verified via a full grep/awk cross-check plus a new automated regression test (TestAllMutatingEndpointsHaveAuth) that walks the live FastAPI route table. Not executed.

findings.location: approve_task, reject_task, complete_task, pipeline_approve, pipeline_reject, push_task, approve_approval, reject_approval
findings.finding: None of these approval-type endpoints import or depend on require_approver. Only epics.py's and memory.py's approval endpoints do. fleet_dashboard.py (named explicitly in the audit checklist) also has zero require_approver/auth dependency usage.
findings.evidence: Full reads of tasks.py and approvals.py -- no require_approver anywhere; grep -n "require_approver" backend/app/api/fleet_dashboard.py returns zero matches.
findings.production_impact: Anyone who can reach the API can approve/reject a task plan, mark a task complete, approve a real git push to GitHub, or approve/reject anything in the fleet dashboard -- the single most consequential action class in the system -- with zero authorization check.
findings.recommendation: Add Depends(require_approver) to every endpoint listed, matching the pattern already correctly used in epics.py/memory.py.
findings.fix_note: require_approver added to all approve/reject/complete/push endpoints in tasks.py, approvals.py, and fleet_dashboard.py. Not executed.

findings.finding: jwt_auth_enabled defaults to False (its own config description literally states the X-User-Role header is accepted as a fallback when false). When JWT is disabled, require_approver accepts any request with header X-User-Role: approver (or admin) with zero verification.
findings.evidence: rbac.py:54-85 full function body; config.py:488-491 default False with the fallback behavior stated in its own description field.
findings.production_impact: In the default configuration, any HTTP client can add one header to instantly satisfy require_approver on the few endpoints that check it at all. Combined with SEC-05-013, RBAC provides real protection on almost nothing.
findings.recommendation: Gate the X-User-Role fallback behind an explicit opt-in flag defaulting to False, or default jwt_auth_enabled=True with a loud startup failure if jwt_secret_key is unset.
findings.fix_note: Added allow_legacy_role_header config field, default False, gating the X-User-Role shortcut in both rbac.py's require_approver and a second, independently-discovered duplicate in auth/dependencies.py's get_current_user. Not executed.

findings.finding: default_admin_password defaults to the hardcoded string "gridiron123". On every startup (gated only on jwt_secret_key being set), the admin user's password is reseeded to this value if it doesn't currently match -- silently reverting any manual password change made through any means other than overriding the DEFAULT_ADMIN_PASSWORD env var.
findings.evidence: config.py:492-495; main.py:277-318 full re-seed block, comment at line 295 states the re-seed-on-mismatch intent explicitly.
findings.production_impact: Any deployment that sets JWT_SECRET_KEY but forgets to also override DEFAULT_ADMIN_PASSWORD has a permanent, unremovable admin/gridiron123 login with role=approver -- full approval rights over every correctly-gated endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Seed the admin account only once (first-ever startup), never overwrite an existing admin row's password automatically. Force a password change on first login. Fail startup loudly if JWT_AUTH_ENABLED=true and the password is still the literal default.
findings.fix_note: Admin now seeded only if no admin row exists at all; freshly-seeded row carries must_change_password: True. Added a real authenticated POST /api/auth/change-password endpoint plus must_change_password in the login response. Not executed.

findings.location: make_coder_handlers.bash, make_chat_handlers.bash, and every shell=True bash handler
findings.finding: Command policy is a blocklist of known-bad patterns, not an allowlist or sandbox. A single bash call containing `cd /other/path && <cmd>` or an absolute path outside the worktree is not blocked unless the specific text matches one of ~23 denylist regexes -- none of which is a generic worktree-containment rule for command text (only write_file/edit_file's path *arguments* get that check).
findings.evidence: tools.py:919-927 (subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, cwd=worktree_path, ...) with cmd as unconstrained free text); policy/engine.py:126-152 has no generic containment rule for command content.
findings.production_impact: Any coder-class or chat agent can, via a non-denylisted but still crafted command, read/write files anywhere the host OS process can reach, not just the worktree. Root cause underlying the Phase 4 prompt-injection risk (SEC-05-018).
findings.recommendation: Run agent bash tool calls inside real OS-level sandboxing (container/gVisor/firejail) scoped to the worktree -- the only complete fix. Partial mitigation: reject `cd` to paths outside the worktree and absolute paths outside it as command arguments.
findings.fix_note: Added check_command_stays_in_boundary() rejecting `cd <absolute-path>` outside the worktree, wired into both coder and chat bash handlers. Explicitly NOT a full OS-level sandbox -- that remains a genuine, larger, still-open follow-up. Not executed.

findings.finding: cwd = inp.get("cwd") or repo_path -- the LLM-controlled tool input can override the bash tool's working directory to an arbitrary value with no validation it stays within repo_path. Coder-class agents hardcode cwd=worktree_path with no such override.
findings.evidence: tools.py:6566-6567 vs. tools.py:924 (make_coder_handlers.bash hardcodes cwd, never reads inp.get("cwd")).
findings.production_impact: Widens the SEC-05-005 escape surface specifically for the chat agent -- no cd chain needed, cwd can be set directly in the tool call.
findings.recommendation: Remove the inp.get("cwd") override, or validate it resolves (realpath) inside repo_path before use.
findings.fix_note: Removed the inp.get("cwd") override entirely; make_chat_handlers.bash now always uses repo_path, matching every other bash handler. Not executed.

findings.finding: The security job runs `pip-audit -r requirements.txt --ignore-vuln GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5 || true`. The trailing || true means this step always exits 0 regardless of what pip-audit finds.
findings.production_impact: The CI security job cannot ever fail the build or flag reviewers to a real finding, regardless of how many or how severe the CVEs pip-audit discovers -- defeats the job's purpose entirely.
findings.recommendation: Remove || true. Extend --ignore-vuln explicitly per suppressed finding instead of blanket-suppressing the whole job's exit code.
findings.fix_note: Removed || true from the pip-audit CI step; the security job can now actually fail the build. Not executed (CI not run).

findings.file: systemic -- no single file, root cause is SEC-05-005/006
findings.finding: Prompt-injection resistance for coder-class agents relies entirely on the same blocklist-not-sandbox command/path policy found insufficient in Phase 1. No content-provenance tagging, second-pass tool-call classifier, or OS-level sandboxing exists between 'untrusted content enters an agent's context' and 'that agent's tool call executes.'
findings.evidence: Grep for injection/sandbox/provenance/untrusted across app/ returns no dedicated module; SEC-05-005/006's evidence is the enforcement mechanism this risk depends on.
findings.production_impact: A well-crafted prompt injection embedded in a repo file, PR description, or web search result could plausibly induce a downstream coder-class agent to execute a harmful command not on the ~23-pattern denylist.
findings.recommendation: Same structural fix as SEC-05-005 (sandboxing); cheap partial mitigation: explicitly delimit untrusted content in agent prompts as data, not instructions.
findings.fix_note: Same underlying mitigation as SEC-05-005 (boundary check on coder/chat bash tools) narrows the exploitable surface for an injected command, but no content-provenance tagging or second-pass classifier was added -- this remains a genuinely open, larger item, not claimed as closed. Not executed.

findings.finding: Custom secret names are only validated as syntactically-valid env-var identifiers, with no denylist for sensitive/reserved names like DATABASE_URL. The stated 'no agent gets deploy credentials' exclusion is implemented only as two hardcoded .pop() calls for GITHUB_TOKEN/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY at the two launch call sites, not as a name restriction on what can be stored.
findings.evidence: settings.py:184-217 (no name denylist anywhere); credential_vault.py:18-20 (stated design intent); agents.py:460-462/681-683 (the exclusion's actual narrow implementation).
findings.production_impact: A custom secret literally named DATABASE_URL can be created and would be injected unexcluded into every coding agent's bash environment, contradicting the stated design intent -- compounded by this endpoint having no authentication at all (SEC-05-012).
findings.recommendation: Add a case-insensitive name denylist (DATABASE_URL, GITHUB_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, JWT_SECRET_KEY, CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY, etc.) rejected with a 400.
findings.fix_note: Added _RESERVED_SECRET_NAMES case-insensitive denylist (DATABASE_URL, GITHUB_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, JWT_SECRET_KEY, CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY, cloud credential names, etc.), enforced with a 400 in save_custom_secret. Also now requires require_approver per SEC-05-012/013. Not executed.

findings.finding: base_graph.py's execute_tools node -- the policy gate for every tool call by all 72+ run_agent_graph agents -- delegates to app.agents.guardrails, a second, independently-maintained, materially weaker duplicate of policy/engine.py, despite guardrails.py's own docstring falsely claiming to be the single audited implementation. Missing: curl/wget https block, sudo, general terraform, npm/pnpm/yarn publish, vercel/heroku, pipe-to-shell, private-key-file patterns, secrets-substring regex, and any worktree-boundary/realpath check. check_bash_allowlist has no chaining-metachar rejection at all.
findings.evidence: guardrails.py:1-4 (false docstring), 19-36 (16 vs 23 patterns), 45-51 (4-prefix startswith only, no realpath), 65-72 (no chaining check); base_graph.py:40,269-281,592-603.
findings.production_impact: Currently harmless for the agents sampled (SEC-05-003) since their own handlers redundantly apply the strong check -- but structural risk for any future agent relying solely on base_graph.py's generic gate. check_bash_allowlist (the chaining-vulnerable function specifically) has zero real callers today, confirmed by grep -- dormant, not live.
findings.recommendation: Delete guardrails.py and import directly from app.policy.engine in base_graph.py, or make guardrails.py a thin re-export instead of a parallel reimplementation. Fix the docstring either way.
findings.fix_note: guardrails.py rewritten to delegate to app.policy.engine's real functions instead of maintaining a separate, weaker denylist; docstring corrected. Not executed.

findings.finding: _is_dangerous_command() gates a confirmation request, not a hard block. If a human approves via request_confirmation, the code executes the original, denylisted command directly with no re-validation, no allowlist, no narrowing -- a human 'approve' click fully overrides the policy engine for this tool.
findings.evidence: tools.py:6569-6604 (confirmation branch) -> tools.py:6605-6619 (unconditional execution regardless of which branch was taken).
findings.production_impact: May be an intentional human-in-the-loop design, but is undocumented as such, and is a residual bypass path if the approving human doesn't read the details field carefully or the approval is triggered by an automated/compromised session.
findings.recommendation: Document the override behavior explicitly in the UI, or narrow the set of patterns that remain non-overridable regardless of confirmation (e.g. rm -rf /, fork bombs, dd if=).
findings.fix_note: Added is_command_override_eligible() -- rm -rf, dd if=, mkfs, shutdown, reboot, fork bomb, and direct device writes now stay hard-blocked even after a human clicks approve in the chat agent's confirmation flow. Not executed.
